NGC 7293 in Aquarius is a planetary nebula about 650 light-years away, among the closest known, and it is not a planet at all: it is the shed outer layers of a Sun-like star that has run out of fuel, blown off over some ten thousand years and lit from within by the hot white dwarf left behind at the centre. The blue-green interior is doubly ionised oxygen, and the red ring around it is hydrogen and nitrogen in the outer shell, where the ejected gas is thinning out; seen in a long exposure the ring is really a tilted cylinder or pair of rings, viewed almost end-on. At roughly 2.5 light-years across it spans about half the width of the Moon, which makes it one of the largest planetary nebulae in the sky. Karl Ludwig Harding discovered it before 1824, and its popular name, the Eye of God, comes from how closely it resembles a human iris.
